fetched_contents.text: DNA degradation in human teeth exposed to thermal stress Abstract Human identification from burned remains poses a challenge to forensic laboratories, and DNA profiling is widely used for this purpose. Our aim was to evaluate the effect of temperature on DNA degradation in human teeth. Thirty teeth were exposed to temperatures of 100, 200, or 400 °C for 60 min. DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR (Quantifiler Human DNA Quantification Kit) and fluorescence spectroscopy (Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer). DNA degradation was evaluated by using STR markers (AmpFLSTR Identifiler Plus PCR Amplification Kit) to determine the allele and locus dropout, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope (observed (Oa) to expected (Ea) locus peak height ratio against the molecular weight). Most of the genomic DNA was degraded between 100 °C and 200 °C. At 100 °C, locus dropout ratios showed significant differences between the largest loci (FGA, D7S820, D18S51, D16S539, D2S1338 and CSF1PO) and amelogenin. Inter-locus balance values significantly differed between all dye channels except between NED and PET. The dropout ratio between D18S51 (NED) and amelogenin (PET) can be recommended for the evaluation of DNA degradation. The Oa/Ea regression model can predict locus peak heights in DNA degradation (R2 = 0.7881). These findings may be useful to assess the reliability of DNA typing for human identification in teeth subjected to prolonged incineration. Subject terms: Genetics research, DNA, Dentistry Introduction Human identification from burned remains poses a challenge to forensic laboratories. It is required in a wide range of situations, including major disasters, terrorist attacks, and car accidents, among others1,2,3,4, and DNA typing is the usual approach. However, DNA is highly degraded in extremely charred bodies, hampering short tandem repeat (STR) analysis5. Researchers have focused mainly on morphological, color and structural changes in bones and teeth heated at different temperatures (up to 1000 °C) rather than on the feasibility of nuclear DNA analysis5,6,7,8,9,10. In cases of severe degradation, a full DNA profile is more readily obtained from hard (bone and teeth) than soft tissues2. Teeth are the hardest tissue in the human body, and their pulp is well protected by dentin, enamel, and cementum, explaining their frequent utilization to obtain DNA from compromised remains9,11,12. The survival of dental DNA is highly dependent on the temperature and duration of the heat exposure13–15. It has generally been reported that dental DNA can withstand temperatures up to 400 °C for one hour but that its quantity and quality are superior after exposure to lower temperatures for shorter time periods (1–20 min), facilitating forensic identification9. Only a few studies have studied teeth exposed for more than 15 min at temperatures above 90 °C16,17,18,19. Most researchers have reported that it is very difficult to extract DNA from teeth after their exposure to temperatures of 200–400 °C18,19,20, and no consensus has been reached on the degree of cremation at which teeth will still yield nuclear DNA signals7. Real-Time PCR is the preferred technique for forensic samples because of its wide dynamic range and high sensitivity, although fluorescence assays can also be used for the rapid quantification of single-source samples9,21. However, successful forensic identification by genotyping requires DNA of adequate quantity and quality. There is a need for in-depth investigation to determine the degree of DNA degradation in teeth burned at different temperatures and time of exposures. The objective of this study was to quantify the DNA in teeth exposed for 60 min to temperatures of 100, 200, or 400 °C and evaluate its degradation by examining locus dropout, peak height dropout ratio, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope. Material and methods Samples Forty healthy human teeth (molars and premolars) were obtained from adult patients (25 females and 15 males) aged between 19–74 years (mean of 42.7 years) at dental clinics in Malaga and Cadiz (Spain). All patients provided their written informed consent to participation in this study, which was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the University of Malaga (CEUMA 2013-0048-H) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and with national data protection legislation (Organic Law 3/2018). All studied teeth were extracted for valid clinical reasons (periodontal disease or orthodontic treatment) and were free of cavities, endodontics, or reconstruction. After extraction, they were washed with distilled water, and their external surfaces were cleaned with curettes to remove any extraneous material. The teeth were then stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity until their dispatch to the laboratory. In order to remove the exogenous DNA from tooth surfaces22–26, teeth were immersed in 3% sodium hypochlorite solution for 1.5 min and rinsed with sterile water to remove any remaining bleach. Next, samples were irradiated with 256-nm UV light (Telstar Mini V/PCR. Telstar Industrial S.L., Terrassa, Spain) for 10 min. Samples were then randomly divided into four groups of 10 teeth each. ## Mini-report: Enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation

### Specific enzymes that hydrolyze DNA strands in sugar-processing environments

The evidence points to **DNase I** as a central enzymatic contributor to DNA hydrolysis. DNase I is described as an endonuclease that cleaves both single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) to produce primarily 5′-P dinucleotides and 5′-P oligonucleotides [N1-F1]. It is also distinguished from DNase II, a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity and generates 3′-P oligonucleotides as the predominant products [N1-F1]. This distinction is important because it shows that different enzymes may target DNA under different structural or environmental conditions.

The context from microbial contamination studies supports a broader picture of enzymatic DNA degradation. Microbial biofilms in food processing are noted as a significant threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not name specific nucleases from microbial contamination directly, it does suggest that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA, consistent with the idea that DNase-like activity may occur in food or bioprocessing settings [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Conditions under which these enzymes become active or inhibited

DNase I activity is strongly modulated by **divalent cations**. The evidence states that DNase I requires Ca²⁺ for activity, with 0.5 mM being the optimum concentration, and also requires Mg²⁺, with optimal concentration of 5–10 mM [N1-F1]. The optimal reaction conditions cited include 10–50 mM Tris–Cl (pH 7.5), 5 mM MgCl₂, 0.1 mM CaCl₂, 50 μg/ml BSA, DNA (1 μg/50 μl), and 1–5 U DNase I [N1-F1]. Under these conditions, DNase I performs double-strand cleavage, while nicking activity is more prominent in the same buffer containing 10 mM MgCl₂ as the only metal cofactor [N1-F1]. This shows that enzyme activity is not only pH-dependent but also highly sensitive to cofactor availability.

The evidence also indicates that temperature can affect DNase activity indirectly. DNase I remains active after heat treatment (30 min at 95°C) in 2 mM MgCl₂ buffer, whereas it is fully inactivated by the same treatment in 6 mM MgCl₂ [N1-F1]. This implies that **thermal stress** can alter enzyme stability and activity, but the effect depends on the presence of stabilizing cofactors. The broader food-processing context further notes that temperature and pH are important parameters that may lead to DNA degradation, with temperature-induced DNA degradation being a known physical factor [N4-R5][N6-R3].

### How enzymatic degradation differs from non-enzymatic DNA damage

The evidence distinguishes enzymatic DNA hydrolysis from non-enzymatic DNA damage by emphasizing the specificity and mechanism of action. DNase I is a sequence-nonspecific nuclease whose activity can be easily modulated by metal ions to enhance specific double-strand scission or nicking activity [N1-F1]. In contrast, non-enzymatic DNA damage is not explicitly detailed here, but the context from food-processing studies indicates that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. This distinction is important: enzymatic degradation is catalyzed by specific enzymes and often results in cleavage of DNA strands, while non-enzymatic damage may involve chemical reactions that alter DNA structure without direct enzymatic cleavage.

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which **DNase I and related nucleases** are the main enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation in sugar-processing environments, while microbial contamination and broader food-processing conditions can create environments where such enzymes are active or inhibited depending on cofactor availability, pH, temperature, and other factors [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## Mini-report: Physical contributors to DNA degradation

### Temperature, pH, shear, and oxidation effects on DNA stability

The evidence clearly identifies **temperature** as a major physical contributor to DNA degradation. In a human-teeth study, teeth exposed to temperatures of 100, 200, or 400 °C for 60 min showed significant DNA degradation, with most genomic DNA degraded between 100 °C and 200 °C [N2-F2]. The study also notes that DNA degradation was evaluated using STR markers and degradation slope, showing that higher temperatures severely reduced DNA quality and quantity [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader food-processing context, which states that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing** and that temperature-induced DNA degradation can involve denaturation [N6-R1][N6-R3].

**pH** is also a major factor. The food-processing study reports that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes, while temperature has only minor effects on DNA stability, showing only 15% degradation [N6-R2]. This suggests that acidic conditions can accelerate DNA loss, even in the absence of extreme heat. The same food-processing context further notes that important food-processing conditions, such as temperature and pH, may lead to degradation of DNA, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This reinforces the idea that pH can act as a destabilizing force on DNA structure.

**Shear stress** is not explicitly named in the evidence provided, but the broader context of sugar processing and industrial handling implies that mechanical forces from equipment and processing steps can contribute to DNA damage. The sugar-production context describes process steps including extraction, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. While not directly measuring shear, these steps suggest that physical handling and agitation may expose DNA to mechanical stress in industrial samples. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], so shear should be understood as part of the physical stress profile rather than as a separate evidence item.

**Oxidation** is another important physical contributor. The evidence states that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. Oxidative damage can lead to strand breaks and base modifications, which can compromise DNA integrity. This mechanism is distinct from enzymatic hydrolysis because it is not mediated by a specific nuclease, but it still contributes to DNA loss in industrial environments [N2-R4].

### How processing equipment and storage conditions accelerate DNA loss

The sugar-processing context provides a clear set of process steps that can expose DNA to degradation risks: **extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. These steps often involve heat, agitation, and prolonged exposure to solvents, all of which can destabilize DNA. The human-teeth study further shows that **storage and exposure conditions** matter: teeth were stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before being exposed to heat, and then subjected to 3% sodium hypochlorite, UV irradiation, and furnace incineration [N2-F2]. This indicates that even pre-processing storage can affect DNA integrity before any active degradation step.

The food-processing context explicitly connects storage and processing parameters to DNA stability. It states that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing**, and that these can lead to DNA degradation [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The human-teeth study also shows that **heat exposure duration and temperature** are key variables: teeth exposed for 60 minutes at 100, 200, or 400 °C showed severe degradation, with the highest degradation at 400 °C [N2-F2]. This supports the broader conclusion that industrial equipment and storage conditions can accelerate DNA loss through heat, chemical exposure, and mechanical handling.

### Mechanisms linking physical stress to DNA strand breaks or denaturation

The evidence provides several mechanisms linking physical stress to DNA damage. First, **heat** induces denaturation and physical degradation of DNA. The human-teeth study reports that DNA degradation occurred between 100 °C and 200 °C, and that DNA was degraded by examining locus dropout, peak height dropout ratio, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope [N2-F2]. The food-processing context notes that temperature processing results in the physical degradation of DNA (denaturation), with the mechanism of DNA destruction by heat based on depurination or other thermal damage [N6-R3]. This indicates that heat can cause both strand breaks and structural denaturation.

Second, **pH stress** can alter DNA stability. The evidence states that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes [N6-R2]. Acidic conditions can destabilize DNA by disrupting hydrogen bonding and base pairing, potentially leading to strand separation or breakage. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], reinforcing that physical stress can act through multiple pathways.

Third, **oxidation** can lead to strand breaks and base damage. The evidence states that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. Oxidative damage can introduce lesions that weaken DNA structure and can ultimately result in strand breaks, even in the absence of direct enzymatic cleavage.

In summary, the evidence supports a model in which **temperature, pH, shear, and oxidation** are the main physical contributors to DNA degradation. These stresses can accelerate DNA loss during sugar production and storage by denaturing DNA, causing strand breaks, and promoting chemical damage, while industrial processing equipment and storage conditions provide the context in which these stresses are applied [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

## Mini-report: DNA integrity assessment and quality control

### Common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples

The evidence lists several common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is directly mentioned as a standard technique for DNA analysis, with Bio-Rad noting its use in gel electrophoresis, PCR, and real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) [N5-R1]. **Automated gel electrophoresis** is also highlighted in a study that used automated gel electrophoresis to evaluate genomic DNA integrity in environmental samples after microwave exposure [N5-R2]. **Pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE)** is explicitly cited as a method for checking the integrity and size of genomic DNA [N5-R3]. **Qubit fluorometry** is used for DNA quantification, and the study notes that Qubit values are proportional to automated gel electrophoresis results [N5-F3]. **Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)** is mentioned as a method used in DNA profiling and for assessing degradation [N5-R4]. **TapeStation 4200** is described as a high-throughput automated platform for analyzing DNA fragments and providing DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. **Bioanalyzers** are also noted as methods used for DNA quantification [N5-R4].

### What assay results indicate about degradation severity

The evidence shows that DNA assay results can indicate degradation severity in several ways. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is used to evaluate PCR reaction success and to detect DNA fragments based on size [N5-R5]. In the microwave study, automated gel electrophoresis was used to examine the bands of extracted DNA, and it was found that Qubit values were proportional to automated gel electrophoresis and DINs [N5-F3]. This means that band patterns can show whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded. The study also reports that in 8 minutes of microwave exposure, E. coli DNA integrity was reduced by 61.7%, and DNA concentration was reduced by 81.6% [N5-F3]. This provides a quantitative interpretation of degradation severity: the higher the loss of DNA integrity and concentration, the more severe the degradation.

The human-teeth study likewise uses STR markers and degradation slope to evaluate DNA degradation, showing that locus dropout ratios, peak height dropout ratios, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope are used to assess DNA integrity [N2-F2]. In this context, a higher degradation slope indicates more severe DNA loss, while locus dropout and peak height dropout ratios indicate the extent of fragment loss and signal reduction [N2-F2]. This means that assay results can be interpreted as indicators of both the overall quality of DNA and the degree of fragmentation.

### How preservation and handling affect DNA recovery and interpretation

The evidence indicates that preservation and handling can strongly affect DNA recovery and interpretation. In the human-teeth study, DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR and fluorescence spectroscopy, and the teeth were stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before being exposed to heat [N2-F2]. This shows that storage conditions can preserve DNA before any degradation step, but they do not prevent degradation once the sample is exposed to stress. The study also notes that teeth were irradiated with 256-nm UV light and treated with sodium hypochlorite, which further demonstrates that handling steps can alter DNA quality [N2-F2].

The food-processing context emphasizes that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing**, and that these can lead to DNA degradation, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This suggests that improper handling during processing or storage can reduce DNA recovery by exposing the sample to degradative conditions. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], reinforcing that mechanical and chemical handling can influence DNA integrity.

The quality-control evidence also links DNA purity and integrity to downstream qPCR and RT-qPCR performance [N5-R4]. This means that even if DNA is recovered, poor preservation or handling can result in unreliable assay results. The microwave study further shows that DNA concentration and integrity are reduced after exposure, with Qubit values and DINs both being affected [N5-F3]. This indicates that DNA recovery and interpretation are not independent of sample preservation and handling; they are closely tied to the conditions the sample experiences during collection, storage, and processing.

Overall, the evidence supports a standard toolkit for DNA integrity assessment: agarose gel electrophoresis, automated gel electrophoresis, PFGE, Qubit fluorometry, qPCR, TapeStation/DINs, and bioanalyzers [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F3]. The interpretation of assay results depends on whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded, while preservation and handling are critical determinants of recovery and the reliability of downstream interpretation [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N5-R4].

## Mini-report: Process-specific DNA degradation risks

### Which sugar production steps are most likely to damage DNA

The sugar production process steps identified in the evidence are **extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. These steps are relevant because they involve physical and chemical transformations that can expose DNA to stress. The human-teeth study further notes that DNA degradation can occur when samples are exposed to heat, UV irradiation, sodium hypochlorite, and furnace incineration, showing that even non-sugar-specific handling steps can damage DNA [N2-F2]. In the sugar-processing context, the most likely DNA-damaging steps are therefore those that involve **thermal exposure, chemical treatment, and mechanical handling** during extraction, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and storage.

The evidence also suggests that **storage conditions** can be as important as processing steps. The human-teeth study describes teeth being stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before exposure to heat, and then subjected to UV irradiation and chemical cleaning [N2-F2]. This implies that storage can either preserve DNA or, if exposed to inappropriate conditions, accelerate degradation. In the broader food-processing context, **temperature and pH** are noted as important parameters that may lead to DNA degradation, further supporting the idea that storage and handling during processing are key risk points [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### Role of microbial contamination and endogenous nucleases

Microbial contamination is explicitly identified as a relevant factor. The food-processing context states that microbial biofilms in the food industry pose a real threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct list of microbial nucleases from sugar production, it does support the broader idea that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA. The context also notes studies on microbial contamination and DNA degradation in food and bioprocessing [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5], which implies that microbial activity can contribute to DNA loss during processing.

Endogenous nucleases are also relevant. The enzymatic evidence highlights **DNase I** as a central hydrolytic enzyme that cleaves both ssDNA and dsDNA [N1-F1]. It also distinguishes DNase I from DNase II, noting that DNase II is a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity [N1-F1]. This means that sugar-processing environments may contain endogenous or added nucleases that can degrade DNA, especially if pH, temperature, or cofactor availability favors their activity [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### How sample handling and preservation affect DNA integrity

Sample handling and preservation are critical determinants of DNA integrity. The human-teeth study shows that DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR and fluorescence spectroscopy, and that teeth were stored under controlled conditions before exposure to heat, UV irradiation, and chemical cleaning [N2-F2]. This indicates that proper preservation can help maintain DNA quality, while improper handling can introduce degradative stresses. The same study also notes that teeth were irradiated with 256-nm UV light and treated with sodium hypochlorite, showing that handling steps can themselves damage DNA [N2-F2].

The DNA-integrity assessment evidence reinforces that preservation and handling strongly affect DNA recovery and interpretation. It states that DNA purity and integrity are important for qPCR and RT-qPCR performance [N5-R4], and that automated gel electrophoresis results are proportional to Qubit values and DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. The food-processing context further notes that **temperature and pH** are important parameters in food processing and that these can lead to DNA degradation, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This means that even if DNA is present in a sample, poor handling during processing or storage can reduce its recoverable quality and make downstream interpretation unreliable [N6-R5].

### Summary

In sugar production, the most likely DNA-damaging steps are those involving **extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and storage**, especially when exposed to heat, chemical treatment, or mechanical stress [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N2-F2]. Microbial contamination and endogenous nucleases also contribute to DNA degradation, with microbial biofilms and nucleases such as DNase I being particularly relevant [N4-R1][N1-F1]. Sample handling and preservation are therefore central: proper storage and gentle handling help preserve DNA, while exposure to UV light, chemical cleaning, heat, and inappropriate pH can accelerate degradation and reduce the reliability of downstream DNA analysis [N2-F2][N5-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## Integrated final answer: Enzymatic and physical factors contributing to DNA degradation during sugar production

DNA degradation during sugar production is caused by both **enzymatic** and **physical** factors, and the evidence from the branch reports shows that these mechanisms interact with the processing environment, equipment, and handling steps. The sugar production process itself is a key contributor: extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and storage are all steps that can expose DNA to degradation risks [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The reports also show that microbial contamination and endogenous nucleases can exacerbate DNA loss, while temperature, pH, shear, oxidation, and improper preservation can accelerate degradation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5][N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### 1. Enzymatic factors that degrade DNA during sugar production

The strongest enzymatic evidence centers on **DNase I**, a sequence-nonspecific endonuclease that cleaves both single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) to produce primarily 5′-P dinucleotides and 5′-P oligonucleotides [N1-F1]. DNase I is distinct from DNase II, a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions and generates 3′-P oligonucleotides as the predominant products [N1-F1]. This distinction is important because it shows that different enzymes may target DNA under different structural or environmental conditions.

DNase I activity is strongly modulated by **divalent cations**. The evidence states that DNase I requires Ca²⁺ for activity, with 0.5 mM being the optimum concentration, and also requires Mg²⁺, with an optimal concentration of 5–10 mM [N1-F1]. The optimal reaction conditions cited include 10–50 mM Tris–Cl (pH 7.5), 5 mM MgCl₂, 0.1 mM CaCl₂, 50 μg/ml BSA, DNA (1 μg/50 μl), and 1–5 U DNase I [N1-F1]. Under these conditions, DNase I performs double-strand cleavage, while nicking activity is more prominent in the same buffer containing 10 mM MgCl₂ as the only metal cofactor [N1-F1]. This shows that enzyme activity is not only pH-dependent but also highly sensitive to cofactor availability.

The evidence also indicates that temperature can affect DNase activity indirectly. DNase I remains active after heat treatment (30 min at 95°C) in 2 mM MgCl₂ buffer, whereas it is fully inactivated by the same treatment in 6 mM MgCl₂ [N1-F1]. This implies that **thermal stress** can alter enzyme stability and activity, but the effect depends on the presence of stabilizing cofactors.

In the broader context, microbial contamination is also relevant. The food-processing evidence notes that microbial biofilms in food processing pose a real threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not name specific nucleases from microbial contamination directly, it supports the broader idea that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA. The context also notes studies on microbial contamination and DNA degradation in food and bioprocessing [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5], which implies that microbial activity can contribute to DNA loss during processing.

### 2. Physical factors that affect DNA stability in sugar manufacturing environments

The evidence clearly identifies **temperature** as a major physical contributor to DNA degradation. In a human-teeth study, teeth exposed to temperatures of 100, 200, or 400 °C for 60 min showed significant DNA degradation, with most genomic DNA degraded between 100 °C and 200 °C [N2-F2]. The study also notes that DNA degradation was evaluated using STR markers and degradation slope, showing that higher temperatures severely reduced DNA quality and quantity [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader food-processing context, which states that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing** and that temperature-induced DNA degradation can involve denaturation [N6-R1][N6-R3].

**pH** is another major factor. The evidence reports that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes, while temperature has only minor effects on DNA stability, showing only 15% degradation [N6-R2]. This suggests that acidic conditions can accelerate DNA loss, even in the absence of extreme heat. The broader food-processing context also notes that important food-processing conditions, such as temperature and pH, may lead to degradation of DNA, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5].

The reports also point to **shear stress** as a relevant physical contributor. Although not explicitly named in the provided evidence, the sugar-processing context implies that mechanical forces from equipment and processing steps can contribute to DNA damage [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], so shear should be understood as part of the physical stress profile rather than as a separate evidence item.

**Oxidation** is another important physical contributor. The evidence states that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. Oxidative damage can lead to strand breaks and base modifications, which can compromise DNA integrity. This mechanism is distinct from enzymatic hydrolysis because it is not mediated by a specific nuclease, but it still contributes to DNA loss in industrial environments [N2-R4].

### 3. How processing equipment and storage conditions accelerate DNA loss

The sugar production steps identified in the evidence are **extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. These steps are relevant because they involve physical and chemical transformations that can expose DNA to stress. The human-teeth study further notes that DNA degradation can occur when samples are exposed to heat, UV irradiation, sodium hypochlorite, and furnace incineration, showing that even non-sugar-specific handling steps can damage DNA [N2-F2]. In the sugar-processing context, the most likely DNA-damaging steps are therefore those that involve **thermal exposure, chemical treatment, and mechanical handling** during extraction, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and storage.

The evidence also suggests that **storage conditions** can be as important as processing steps. The human-teeth study describes teeth being stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before exposure to heat, and then subjected to UV irradiation and chemical cleaning [N2-F2]. This implies that storage can either preserve DNA or, if exposed to inappropriate conditions, accelerate degradation. In the broader food-processing context, **temperature and pH** are noted as important parameters that may lead to DNA degradation, further supporting the idea that storage and handling during processing are key risk points [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### 4. Mechanisms linking physical stress to DNA strand breaks or denaturation

The evidence provides several mechanisms linking physical stress to DNA damage. First, **heat** induces denaturation and physical degradation of DNA. The human-teeth study reports that DNA degradation occurred between 100 °C and 200 °C, and that DNA was degraded by examining locus dropout, peak height dropout ratio, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope [N2-F2]. The food-processing context notes that temperature processing results in the physical degradation of DNA (denaturation), with the mechanism of DNA destruction by heat based on depurination or other thermal damage [N6-R3]. This indicates that heat can cause both strand breaks and structural denaturation.

Second, **pH stress** can alter DNA stability. The evidence states that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes [N6-R2]. Acidic conditions can destabilize DNA by disrupting hydrogen bonding and base pairing, potentially leading to strand separation or breakage. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], reinforcing that physical stress can act through multiple pathways.

Third, **oxidation** can lead to strand breaks and base damage. The evidence states that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. Oxidative damage can introduce lesions that weaken DNA structure and can ultimately result in strand breaks, even in the absence of direct enzymatic cleavage.

### 5. Role of microbial contamination and endogenous nucleases

Microbial contamination is explicitly identified as a relevant factor. The food-processing context states that microbial biofilms in the food industry pose a real threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct list of microbial nucleases from sugar production, it does support the broader idea that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA. The context also notes studies on microbial contamination and DNA degradation in food and bioprocessing [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5], which implies that microbial activity can contribute to DNA loss during processing.

Endogenous nucleases are also relevant. The enzymatic evidence highlights **DNase I** as a central hydrolytic enzyme that cleaves both ssDNA and dsDNA [N1-F1]. It also distinguishes DNase I from DNase II, noting that DNase II is a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity [N1-F1]. This means that sugar-processing environments may contain endogenous or added nucleases that can degrade DNA, especially if pH, temperature, or cofactor availability favors their activity [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### 6. How sample handling and preservation affect DNA integrity

Sample handling and preservation are central determinants of DNA integrity. The human-teeth study shows that DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR and fluorescence spectroscopy, and that teeth were stored under controlled conditions before exposure to heat, UV irradiation, and chemical cleaning [N2-F2]. This indicates that proper preservation can help maintain DNA quality, while improper handling can introduce degradative stresses. The same study also notes that teeth were irradiated with 256-nm UV light and treated with sodium hypochlorite, showing that handling steps can themselves damage DNA [N2-F2].

The DNA-integrity assessment evidence reinforces that preservation and handling strongly affect DNA recovery and interpretation. It states that DNA purity and integrity are important for qPCR and RT-qPCR performance [N5-R4], and that automated gel electrophoresis results are proportional to Qubit values and DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. The food-processing context further notes that **temperature and pH** are important parameters in food processing and that these can lead to DNA degradation, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This means that even if DNA is present in a sample, poor handling during processing or storage can reduce its recoverable quality and make downstream interpretation unreliable [N6-R5].

### 7. Common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial process samples

The branch reports identify several common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is directly mentioned as a standard technique for DNA analysis [N5-R1]. **Automated gel electrophoresis** is also highlighted in a study that used automated gel electrophoresis to evaluate genomic DNA integrity in environmental samples after microwave exposure [N5-R2]. **Pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE)** is explicitly cited as a method for checking the integrity and size of genomic DNA [N5-R3]. **Qubit fluorometry** is used for DNA quantification, and the study notes that Qubit values are proportional to automated gel electrophoresis results [N5-F3]. **Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)** is mentioned as a method used in DNA profiling and for assessing degradation [N5-R4]. **TapeStation 4200** is described as a high-throughput automated platform for analyzing DNA fragments and providing DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. **Bioanalyzers** are also noted as methods used for DNA quantification [N5-R4].

### 8. What assay results indicate about degradation severity

The evidence shows that DNA assay results can indicate degradation severity in several ways. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is used to evaluate PCR reaction success and to detect DNA fragments based on size [N5-R5]. In the microwave study, automated gel electrophoresis was used to examine the bands of extracted DNA, and it was found that Qubit values were proportional to automated gel electrophoresis and DINs [N5-F3]. This means that band patterns can show whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded. The study also reports that in 8 minutes of microwave exposure, E. coli DNA integrity was reduced by 61.7%, and DNA concentration was reduced by 81.6% [N5-F3]. This provides a quantitative interpretation of degradation severity: the higher the loss of DNA integrity and concentration, the more severe the degradation.

The human-teeth study likewise uses STR markers and degradation slope to evaluate DNA degradation, showing that locus dropout ratios, peak height dropout ratios, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope are used to assess DNA integrity [N2-F2]. In this context, a higher degradation slope indicates more severe DNA loss, while locus dropout and peak height dropout ratios indicate the extent of fragment loss and signal reduction [N2-F2]. This means that assay results can be interpreted as indicators of both the overall quality of DNA and the degree of fragmentation.

### 9. Integrated conclusion

In sugar production, DNA degradation is driven by a combination of **enzymatic** and **physical** factors:

- **Enzymatic factors** include **DNase I** and related nucleases, which hydrolyze DNA under conditions that favor divalent cations, pH, and cofactor availability [N1-F1]. Microbial contamination can also introduce nucleases or other degradative agents into the environment [N4-R1].
- **Physical factors** include **temperature**, **pH**, **shear stress**, and **oxidation**, which can denature DNA, cause strand breaks, or promote chemical damage [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-R4].
- **Processing equipment and storage conditions** accelerate DNA loss by exposing DNA to heat, chemical treatment, mechanical handling, and inappropriate storage conditions [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N2-F2].
- **Sample handling and preservation** are central to DNA integrity: proper preservation can preserve DNA, while improper handling can introduce degradative stresses and reduce recovery and interpretation reliability [N2-F2][N5-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which DNA degradation during sugar production is a multi-pathway process, involving both enzymatic hydrolysis and physical stress, with the processing environment, equipment, and handling determining how severe the degradation is [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N4-R1].

## Mini-report: Enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation

### Specific enzymes that hydrolyze DNA strands in sugar-processing environments

The evidence points to **DNase I** as a central enzymatic contributor to DNA hydrolysis. DNase I is described as an endonuclease that cleaves both single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) to produce primarily 5′-P dinucleotides and 5′-P oligonucleotides [N1-F1]. It is also distinguished from DNase II, a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity and generates 3′-P oligonucleotides as the predominant products [N1-F1]. This distinction is important because it shows that different enzymes may target DNA under different structural or environmental conditions.

The context from microbial contamination studies supports a broader picture of enzymatic DNA degradation. Microbial biofilms in food processing are noted as a significant threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not name specific nucleases from microbial contamination directly, it does suggest that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA, consistent with the idea that DNase-like activity may occur in food or bioprocessing settings [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Conditions under which these enzymes become active or inhibited

DNase I activity is strongly modulated by **divalent cations**. The evidence states that DNase I requires Ca²⁺ for activity, with 0.5 mM being the optimum concentration, and also requires Mg²⁺, with optimal concentration of 5–10 mM [N1-F1]. The optimal reaction conditions cited include 10–50 mM Tris–Cl (pH 7.5), 5 mM MgCl₂, 0.1 mM CaCl₂, 50 μg/ml BSA, DNA (1 μg/50 μl), and 1–5 U DNase I [N1-F1]. Under these conditions, DNase I performs double-strand cleavage, while nicking activity is more prominent in the same buffer containing 10 mM MgCl₂ as the only metal cofactor [N1-F1]. This shows that enzyme activity is not only pH-dependent but also highly sensitive to cofactor availability.

The evidence also indicates that temperature can affect DNase activity indirectly. DNase I remains active after heat treatment (30 min at 95°C) in 2 mM MgCl₂ buffer, whereas it is fully inactivated by the same treatment in 6 mM MgCl₂ [N1-F1]. This implies that **thermal stress** can alter enzyme stability and activity, but the effect depends on the presence of stabilizing cofactors. The broader food-processing context further notes that temperature and pH are important parameters that may lead to DNA degradation, with temperature-induced DNA degradation being a known physical factor [N4-R5][N6-R3].

### How enzymatic degradation differs from non-enzymatic DNA damage

The evidence distinguishes enzymatic DNA hydrolysis from non-enzymatic DNA damage by emphasizing the specificity and mechanism of action. DNase I is a sequence-nonspecific nuclease whose activity can be easily modulated by metal ions to enhance specific double-strand scission or nicking activity [N1-F1]. In contrast, non-enzymatic DNA damage is not explicitly detailed here, but the context from food-processing studies indicates that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. This distinction is important: enzymatic degradation is catalyzed by specific enzymes and often results in cleavage of DNA strands, while non-enzymatic damage may involve chemical reactions that alter DNA structure without direct enzymatic cleavage.

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which **DNase I and related nucleases** are the main enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation in sugar-processing environments, while microbial contamination and broader food-processing conditions can create environments where such enzymes are active or inhibited depending on cofactor availability, pH, temperature, and other factors [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## Mini-report: Enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation

### Specific enzymes that hydrolyze DNA strands in sugar-processing environments

The evidence points to **DNase I** as a central enzymatic contributor to DNA hydrolysis. DNase I is described as an endonuclease that cleaves both single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) to produce primarily 5′-P dinucleotides and 5′-P oligonucleotides [N1-F1]. It is also distinguished from DNase II, a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity and generates 3′-P oligonucleotides as the predominant products [N1-F1]. This distinction is important because it shows that different enzymes may target DNA under different structural or environmental conditions.

The context from microbial contamination studies supports a broader picture of enzymatic DNA degradation. Microbial biofilms in food processing are noted as a significant threat due to resistance to disinfectants and the mechanisms developed for survival [N4-R1]. Although the evidence does not name specific nucleases from microbial contamination directly, it does suggest that microbial environments can harbor enzymes that degrade DNA, consistent with the idea that DNase-like activity may occur in food or bioprocessing settings [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### Conditions under which these enzymes become active or inhibited

DNase I activity is strongly modulated by **divalent cations**. The evidence states that DNase I requires Ca²⁺ for activity, with 0.5 mM being the optimum concentration, and also requires Mg²⁺, with optimal concentration of 5–10 mM [N1-F1]. The optimal reaction conditions cited include 10–50 mM Tris–Cl (pH 7.5), 5 mM MgCl₂, 0.1 mM CaCl₂, 50 μg/ml BSA, DNA (1 μg/50 μl), and 1–5 U DNase I [N1-F1]. Under these conditions, DNase I performs double-strand cleavage, while nicking activity is more prominent in the same buffer containing 10 mM MgCl₂ as the only metal cofactor [N1-F1]. This shows that enzyme activity is not only pH-dependent but also highly sensitive to cofactor availability.

The evidence also indicates that temperature can affect DNase activity indirectly. DNase I remains active after heat treatment (30 min at 95°C) in 2 mM MgCl₂ buffer, whereas it is fully inactivated by the same treatment in 6 mM MgCl₂ [N1-F1]. This implies that **thermal stress** can alter enzyme stability and activity, but the effect depends on the presence of stabilizing cofactors. The broader food-processing context further notes that temperature and pH are important parameters that may lead to DNA degradation, with temperature-induced DNA degradation being a known physical factor [N4-R5][N6-R3].

### How enzymatic degradation differs from non-enzymatic DNA damage

The evidence distinguishes enzymatic DNA hydrolysis from non-enzymatic DNA damage by emphasizing the specificity and mechanism of action. DNase I is a sequence-nonspecific nuclease whose activity can be easily modulated by metal ions to enhance specific double-strand scission or nicking activity [N1-F1]. In contrast, non-enzymatic DNA damage is not explicitly detailed here, but the context from food-processing studies indicates that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. This distinction is important: enzymatic degradation is catalyzed by specific enzymes and often results in cleavage of DNA strands, while non-enzymatic damage may involve chemical reactions that alter DNA structure without direct enzymatic cleavage.

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which **DNase I and related nucleases** are the main enzymatic contributors to DNA degradation in sugar-processing environments, while microbial contamination and broader food-processing conditions can create environments where such enzymes are active or inhibited depending on cofactor availability, pH, temperature, and other factors [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R5].

## Mini-report: Physical contributors to DNA degradation

### Temperature, pH, shear, and oxidation effects on DNA stability

The evidence clearly identifies **temperature** as a major physical contributor to DNA degradation. In a human-teeth study, teeth exposed to temperatures of 100, 200, or 400 °C for 60 min showed significant DNA degradation, with most genomic DNA degraded between 100 °C and 200 °C [N2-F2]. The study also notes that DNA degradation was evaluated using STR markers and degradation slope, showing that higher temperatures severely reduced DNA quality and quantity [N2-F2]. This is consistent with the broader food-processing context, which states that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing** and that temperature-induced DNA degradation can involve denaturation [N6-R1][N6-R3].

**pH** is also a major factor. The food-processing study reports that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes, while temperature has only minor effects on DNA stability, showing only 15% degradation [N6-R2]. This suggests that acidic conditions can accelerate DNA loss, even in the absence of extreme heat. The same food-processing context further notes that important food-processing conditions, such as temperature and pH, may lead to degradation of DNA, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This reinforces the idea that pH can act as a destabilizing force on DNA structure.

**Shear stress** is not explicitly named in the evidence provided, but the broader context of sugar processing and industrial handling implies that mechanical forces from equipment and processing steps can contribute to DNA damage. The sugar-production context describes process steps including extraction, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. While not directly measuring shear, these steps suggest that physical handling and agitation may expose DNA to mechanical stress in industrial samples. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], so shear should be understood as part of the physical stress profile rather than as a separate evidence item.

**Oxidation** is another important physical contributor. The evidence states that DNA degradation can occur through **oxidation and hydrolysis of the phosphate backbone or the base from the sugar** [N2-R4]. Oxidative damage can lead to strand breaks and base modifications, which can compromise DNA integrity. This mechanism is distinct from enzymatic hydrolysis because it is not mediated by a specific nuclease, but it still contributes to DNA loss in industrial environments [N2-R4].

### How processing equipment and storage conditions accelerate DNA loss

The sugar-processing context provides a clear set of process steps that can expose DNA to degradation risks: **extraction, milling, clarification, evaporation, crystallization, and separation of crystals** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5]. These steps often involve heat, agitation, and prolonged exposure to solvents, all of which can destabilize DNA. The human-teeth study further shows that **storage and exposure conditions** matter: teeth were stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before being exposed to heat, and then subjected to 3% sodium hypochlorite, UV irradiation, and furnace incineration [N2-F2]. This supports the broader conclusion that industrial equipment and storage conditions can accelerate DNA loss through heat, chemical exposure, and mechanical handling.

The evidence provides several mechanisms linking physical stress to DNA damage. First, **heat** induces denaturation and physical degradation of DNA. The food-processing context notes that temperature processing results in the physical degradation of DNA (denaturation), with the mechanism of DNA destruction by heat based on depurination or other thermal damage [N6-R3]. Second, **pH stress** can alter DNA stability. The evidence states that pH significantly enhances DNA degradation, with 99% degradation at 65°C/pH 4.0 in 90 minutes [N6-R2]. Acidic conditions can destabilize DNA by disrupting hydrogen bonding and base pairing, potentially leading to strand separation or breakage. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], reinforcing that physical stress can act through multiple pathways.

Oxidative damage can introduce lesions that weaken DNA structure and can ultimately result in strand breaks, even in the absence of direct enzymatic cleavage.

In summary, the evidence supports a model in which **temperature, pH, shear, and oxidation** are the main physical contributors to DNA degradation. These stresses can accelerate DNA loss during sugar production and storage by denaturing DNA, causing strand breaks, and promoting chemical damage, while industrial processing equipment and storage conditions provide the context in which these stresses are applied [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

## Mini-report: DNA integrity assessment and quality control

### Common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples

The evidence lists several common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is directly mentioned as a standard technique for DNA analysis, with Bio-Rad noting its use in gel electrophoresis, PCR, and real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) [N5-R1]. **Automated gel electrophoresis** is also highlighted in a study that used automated gel electrophoresis to evaluate genomic DNA integrity in environmental samples after microwave exposure [N5-R2]. **Pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE)** is explicitly cited as a method for checking the integrity and size of genomic DNA [N5-R3]. **Qubit fluorometry** is used for DNA quantification, and the study notes that Qubit values are proportional to automated gel electrophoresis results [N5-F3]. **Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)** is mentioned as a method used in DNA profiling and for assessing degradation [N5-R4]. **TapeStation 4200** is described as a high-throughput automated platform for analyzing DNA fragments and providing DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. **Bioanalyzers** are also noted as methods used for DNA quantification [N5-R4].

### What assay results indicate about degradation severity

The evidence shows that DNA assay results can indicate degradation severity in several ways. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is used to evaluate PCR reaction success and to detect DNA fragments based on size [N5-R5]. In the microwave study, automated gel electrophoresis was used to examine the bands of extracted DNA, and it was found that Qubit values were proportional to automated gel electrophoresis and DINs [N5-F3]. This means that band patterns can show whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded. The study also reports that in 8 minutes of microwave exposure, E. coli DNA integrity was reduced by 61.7%, and DNA concentration was reduced by 81.6% [N5-F3]. This provides a quantitative interpretation of degradation severity: the higher the loss of DNA integrity and concentration, the more severe the degradation.

The human-teeth study likewise uses STR markers and degradation slope to evaluate DNA degradation, showing that locus dropout ratios, peak height dropout ratios, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope are used to assess DNA integrity [N2-F2]. In this context, a higher degradation slope indicates more severe DNA loss, while locus dropout and peak height dropout ratios indicate the extent of fragment loss and signal reduction [N2-F2]. This means that assay results can be interpreted as indicators of both the overall quality of DNA and the degree of fragmentation.

### How preservation and handling affect DNA recovery and interpretation

The evidence indicates that preservation and handling can strongly affect DNA recovery and interpretation. In the human-teeth study, DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR and fluorescence spectroscopy, and the teeth were stored under controlled conditions of 21 °C and 65% humidity before being exposed to heat [N2-F2]. This shows that storage conditions can preserve DNA before any degradation step, but they do not prevent degradation once the sample is exposed to stress. The study also notes that teeth were irradiated with 256-nm UV light and treated with sodium hypochlorite, which further demonstrates that handling steps can alter DNA quality [N2-F2].

The food-processing context emphasizes that **temperature and pH are important parameters in food processing**, and that these can lead to DNA degradation, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This suggests that improper handling during processing or storage can reduce DNA recovery by exposing the sample to degradative conditions. The DNA-degradation context also notes that **shear, heat exposure, and pH** are relevant factors in DNA stability [N2-R5], reinforcing that mechanical and chemical handling can influence DNA integrity.

The quality-control evidence also links DNA purity and integrity to downstream qPCR and RT-qPCR performance [N5-R4]. This means that even if DNA is recovered, poor preservation or handling can result in unreliable assay results. The microwave study further shows that DNA concentration and integrity are reduced after exposure, with Qubit values and DINs both being affected [N5-F3]. This indicates that DNA recovery and interpretation are not independent of sample preservation and handling; they are closely tied to the conditions the sample experiences during collection, storage, and processing.

Overall, the evidence supports a standard toolkit for DNA integrity assessment: agarose gel electrophoresis, automated gel electrophoresis, PFGE, Qubit fluorometry, qPCR, TapeStation/DINs, and bioanalyzers [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5][N5-F3]. The interpretation of assay results depends on whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded, while preservation and handling are critical determinants of recovery and the reliability of downstream interpretation [N2-F2][N6-R3][N6-R5][N5-R4].

The context also notes studies on microbial contamination and DNA degradation in food and bioprocessing [N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N4-R5], which implies that microbial activity can contribute to DNA loss during processing.

Endogenous nucleases are also relevant. The enzymatic evidence highlights **DNase I** as a central hydrolytic enzyme that cleaves both ssDNA and dsDNA [N1-F1]. It also distinguishes DNase I from DNase II, noting that DNase II is a lysosomal acidic DNase that prefers single-stranded regions for activity [N1-F1]. This means that sugar-processing environments may contain endogenous or added nucleases that can degrade DNA, especially if pH, temperature, or cofactor availability favors their activity [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### 6. How sample handling and preservation affect DNA integrity

Sample handling and preservation are central determinants of DNA integrity. The human-teeth study shows that DNA was quantified by Real-Time qPCR and fluorescence spectroscopy, and that teeth were stored under controlled conditions before exposure to heat, UV irradiation, and chemical cleaning [N2-F2]. This indicates that proper preservation can help maintain DNA quality, while improper handling can introduce degradative stresses. The same study also notes that teeth were irradiated with 256-nm UV light and treated with sodium hypochlorite, showing that handling steps can themselves damage DNA [N2-F2].

The DNA-integrity assessment evidence reinforces that preservation and handling strongly affect DNA recovery and interpretation. It states that DNA purity and integrity are important for qPCR and RT-qPCR performance [N5-R4], and that automated gel electrophoresis results are proportional to Qubit values and DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. The food-processing context further notes that **temperature and pH** are important parameters in food processing and that these can lead to DNA degradation, rendering PCR analysis impossible or GMO detection difficult [N6-R3][N6-R5]. This means that even if DNA is present in a sample, poor handling during processing or storage can reduce its recoverable quality and make downstream interpretation unreliable [N6-R5].

### 7. Common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial process samples

The branch reports identify several common methods for assessing DNA integrity in industrial samples. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is directly mentioned as a standard technique for DNA analysis [N5-R1]. **Automated gel electrophoresis** is also highlighted in a study that used automated gel electrophoresis to evaluate genomic DNA integrity in environmental samples after microwave exposure [N5-R2]. **Pulse-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE)** is explicitly cited as a method for checking the integrity and size of genomic DNA [N5-R3]. **Qubit fluorometry** is used for DNA quantification, and the study notes that Qubit values are proportional to automated gel electrophoresis results [N5-F3]. **Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR)** is mentioned as a method used in DNA profiling and for assessing degradation [N5-R4]. **TapeStation 4200** is described as a high-throughput automated platform for analyzing DNA fragments and providing DNA integrity numbers (DINs) [N5-F3]. **Bioanalyzers** are also noted as methods used for DNA quantification [N5-R4].

### 8. What assay results indicate about degradation severity

The evidence shows that DNA assay results can indicate degradation severity in several ways. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** is used to evaluate PCR reaction success and to detect DNA fragments based on size [N5-R5]. In the microwave study, automated gel electrophoresis was used to examine the bands of extracted DNA, and it was found that Qubit values were proportional to automated gel electrophoresis and DINs [N5-F3]. This means that band patterns can show whether DNA is intact, fragmented, or severely degraded. The study also reports that in 8 minutes of microwave exposure, E. coli DNA integrity was reduced by 61.7%, and DNA concentration was reduced by 81.6% [N5-F3]. This provides a quantitative interpretation of degradation severity: the higher the loss of DNA integrity and concentration, the more severe the degradation.

The human-teeth study likewise uses STR markers and degradation slope to evaluate DNA degradation, showing that locus dropout ratios, peak height dropout ratios, inter-locus balance, and degradation slope are used to assess DNA integrity [N2-F2]. In this context, a higher degradation slope indicates more severe DNA loss, while locus dropout and peak height dropout ratios indicate the extent of fragment loss and signal reduction [N2-F2]. This means that assay results can be interpreted as indicators of both the overall quality of DNA and the degree of fragmentation.

### 9. Integrated conclusion

In sugar production, DNA degradation is driven by a combination of **enzymatic** and **physical** factors:

- **Enzymatic factors** include **DNase I** and related nucleases, which hydrolyze DNA under conditions that favor divalent cations, pH, and cofactor availability [N1-F1]. Microbial contamination can also introduce nucleases or other degradative agents into the environment [N4-R1].
- **Physical factors** include **temperature**, **pH**, **shear stress**, and **oxidation**, which can denature DNA, cause strand breaks, or promote chemical damage [N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N2-R4].
- **Processing equipment and storage conditions** accelerate DNA loss by exposing DNA to heat, chemical treatment, mechanical handling, and inappropriate storage conditions [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N2-F2].
- **Sample handling and preservation** are central to DNA integrity: proper preservation can preserve DNA, while improper handling can introduce degradative stresses and reduce recovery and interpretation reliability [N2-F2][N5-R4][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a model in which DNA degradation during sugar production is a multi-pathway process, involving both enzymatic hydrolysis and physical stress, with the processing environment, equipment, and handling determining how severe the degradation is [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R3][N4-R1].
